title: Connecting Representations
subtitle: Helping students move fluently among tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and words — and see them as the same idea in different clothes.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: NCTM, Principles to Actions (ETP 2, 2014) · Lesh translation model · Kelemanik & Lucenta, Routines for Reasoning (Connecting Representations).

blocks.text: A focus on **the links between representations** — tables, graphs, equations, diagrams/pictures, and words/context — rather than treating each as a separate skill. Students learn to translate between them and to explain *why* they match.

Deep understanding lives in the connections: a student who sees that the slope in an equation is the same “per-step” change in a table and the same steepness on a graph understands proportional and linear relationships in a way that a student who can only “do” each form never will. This is NCTM Effective Teaching Practice #2, and it’s a recurring move in the **Connecting Representations** instructional routine (Kelemanik & Lucenta).

Mathematical ideas can usually be shown four ways — **numerically (table), graphically, symbolically (equation), and verbally (words/context)** — with a fifth, concrete/visual (diagrams, manipulatives), especially important in 6–8. Understanding is the ability to move among them and justify the match.

blocks.text: What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: “Where is the rate of change in the table? the graph? the equation?”
Students matching a graph to its equation and justifying why
Multiple representations side by side, with links drawn
Students choosing a representation that helps them reason
“These all show the same relationship because…”

no.title: We should not see
items: Each representation taught as an isolated procedure
“Make a table, then make a graph” with no connection drawn
Only ever using equations (the most abstract form)
Representations treated as the goal rather than tools for meaning

blocks.text: It’s common to have students produce a table *and* a graph *and* an equation — and never link them. That’s representations in parallel, not connected. The learning is in the explicit question: “*where* is this feature in each one, and *why*?”

items: **Multiple representations are multiple entry points** — a student who can’t start from an equation can start from a picture or a table, then connect up.
**Visual and concrete forms lower the language load** for multilingual learners while keeping the mathematics rigorous.
**Honoring whichever representation a student reasons with** validates diverse thinking instead of privileging the symbolic.

sections.label: Lesson design connection
sections.sources: Sources: NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) · Kelemanik & Lucenta, Routines for Reasoning · connects to Same But Different & the 5 Practices here.

blocks.text: Where it lives in the lesson
It’s both a **stand-alone routine** and a **habit inside the consolidation** of any rich task — the Connect in the 5 Practices is largely about linking representations.

items: **Show two representations** of the same idea (e.g., a graph and an equation), or a set to be matched.
**Students study them silently,** then turn-and-talk: “How do these connect? Where is ___ in each?”
**Match & justify.** Students pair them and explain the *features* that justify the match (not “it looks right” — “the slope of 2 is the +2 in the table”).
**Create the missing one.** Given a graph, build the table or equation — and say how you knew.
**Name the connection** as a class: where each key feature lives in every form.

rows: A double number line / tape diagram

blocks.text: The whole lesson’s payoff is one question: “The number 3 shows up in all five — *where*, and *why is it the same 3*?” That’s connected understanding.

items: **Pick the connection that carries the concept** (slope across forms; the constant of proportionality; equivalent fractions across area-model and symbol).
**Choose two or three representations** to link — don’t overload.
**Plan the “where is it in each?” question** — that’s the lever.
**Decide what students produce** (a match-and-justify, or create-the-missing-form).

blocks.title: Pairs naturally with Same But Different

blocks.text: The opener routine **Same But Different** (comparing a table to a graph, say) is the bite-sized rehearsal for this. If your faculty runs that opener, connecting representations in Core is a familiar move at larger scale.

items: **Start from the most accessible representation** for your students (often the picture or context) and connect *up* to the symbolic — not the reverse.
**Let students reason in the representation they’re strongest in,** then build the bridge; this is access without lowering rigor.
**Visuals and double number lines** give multilingual learners a non-verbal anchor for the relationship.

blocks.text: Connecting representations is the habit that makes consolidation deep instead of procedural. Build it into every rich-task Connect and run it as a stand-alone routine on key concepts, and students stop seeing math as a pile of separate skills and start seeing the relationships underneath.
